Draft 2 then failed on sources 9, 15 and 16, which are not among this idea's supplied sources; draft 3 states the contact and piping faces as textbook facts with no footnote, words the isolation check without a citation, and restores [^1] (four sources, five footnotes).
keep: The idea is named in two plain sentences up front: a diagram maps what is joined to what, so you read it by its lines, not by where things sit.

Thirteen screens: an opener puzzle (1, three drawings, which is joined differently), then SHOW 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 alternating with DO 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, ending with two mixed puzzles (12, 13). Every lesson 1 misconception in the brief has its own DO screen and hint: layout read as joints (1, 3), crossing taken as a joint (5, 13), lined up means in series (7), a link that seems to do nothing (9), the drawn state taken for the state now (11), reading order (12).

The two count puzzles (5, 13) are typed whole numbers with the crossing slip and the missed-branch slip each named in its hint; the other puzzles choose between named things or say a direction or a state in words, so they stay as options.
Every SHOW screen has one to three plain sentences and, where it asks him to act, a read sentence and a still.
Tags are used as names only (-Q1, -K1, -M1): no screen explains what the letters stand for, since the brief marks those letter meanings unconfirmed.

The drawn-state rule stays at screens 10 and 11, not as the first DO after the opener as the brief sets for later lessons: this lesson is where the rule is taught, so asking it earlier would test a guess.
fix: Causal step skipped: the draft says a diagram is not a picture of the plant but not why parts sit where they do. Say it is drawn to show how the system works, so parts go where their lines are easy to follow.

False absolute: 'A line joins the parts at its ends and at its dots' ignores a line ending on another in a T, which joins with or without a dot. The explanation and practice are read without the ignores panel, so say it there.
False absolute: 'A contact is drawn as it sits with its coil off' covers relay and contactor contacts only. Narrow it to a relay or contactor contact.
Words of time and place: 'every joint stays where it was' is literally false when a symbol is dragged; the joint moves with it. Say 'every joint stays the same'.

The drawn state is wrong for the pump set's pipe valve. A piping diagram shows a valve in its normal position, which can be open with the plant running, so a spring-held solenoid valve on the water pipe cannot honestly be 'shut as drawn'. Make -V1 a hand valve, and put the state card's valve on the air card (-V2, a spring-return solenoid valve, its neutral position shut). Add the piping face of the rule in one sentence with [^15], so the rule is the general one later lessons need: each kind of sheet has its own drawn state.
Crossing rule scope: [^2] is about circuit diagrams. Keep the cited sentence and the practice line to circuit diagrams; the picture's crossing is between two cables.

The misconception is stated, not shown failing, in the explanation. Add the lamp on the motor's frame that is fed from the isolator's line, and the worked count: the line leaving -Q1 reaches 2 parts, the motor not among them.
Too many footnotes once [^15] is added: drop [^1], whose point [^3] already carries, so there is one footnote per rule he would look up.
Sources: add 9, 15 and 16, copied from research.json.
Brief names a non-change only. Name the cause: the same parts light from each line because only the joints carry meaning, however the parts or symbols are dragged.
Screen 9: 'the room shows no such wire' would make the drawing look wrong. Say no such wire is in view, and that a wire out of sight still joins if the drawing shows it.

No recall checks (taught mode, checks empty). Labels: the readout is 23 characters; the long choices ('-E1 in series with -E2 and -E3 in parallel') stack one per row at phone width, so say so in the screen list.
